chapter: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
title: Joining June Clark's band at the 14th Street dancing school
summary: Left in New York, McRae met trumpeter June Clark and joined his band at a dime-a-dance school, where he taught guitarist Lawrence Lucie the ropes.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Yeah, let's go to Buffalo. He wanted to go to Buffalo. I said, 'I don't want to go to Buffalo.' 'Maybe I'll stay around New York for a while.' So, my two oldest brothers, Bill and Floyd, they went to Buffalo. Now they worked around Buffalo -- they had their own little combos around there -- they worked around Buffalo for a long while. They stayed in Buffalo for quite a while. And I stayed in New York. And this is when I met June Clark. He was playing down at a dance -- 14th Street -- a little
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
dancing school. It was very popular, those dancing schools.
You'd come in and buy tickets to dance with the girls, and things like that.
Were those called "dime dances or nickel dances?"
Yeah, dime dances. Yeah, where the guy come in and buy a roll of tickets and dance with the girl two or three dances.
We worked there. June had this -- it was a good band. A real good band, played good music.

You had to play waltzes and everything -- you know, fox trots and everything. And it was a good learning thing, because you got a chance to really learn all the music -- the different styles and things you never even played.
It really was a breaking out point. And I've never forget when we got Lawrence (inaudible) -- I was with him for about six months and we needed a guitar and we brought in Lawrence Lucie.
And Lawrence Lucie was just begin to --

you know Lawrence Lucie, the guitar player? Well anyway, he came and --
I like Lawrence Lucie because he was very anxious to learn. He hadn't (inaudible) or anything. This was all new to him at that time.
I was like an old pro then. I had been there about six months, you know, three months. I was showing Lawrence Lucie how to do this and that.

He writes in his book now how Teddy McRae helped me, stuck with me and he kept me with the band. It was good. It was a real learning -- something that you might say was a dime and dance dance school, but the bands in those schools was really top notch guys. They were really good musicians in those schools.
